title: Deriving zooplankton response diversity from SDMs
summary: In this project we use empirical data on zooplankton communities in reservoirs across Japan to first derive species distribution models and link species occurrence probability to environmental variables. We then simulate species extinctions on these communities and ask whether the response diversity of these communities to various environmental variables can predict reductions in functional diversity and functional "robustness".
drivers: Temperature, land use characteristics, predation pressure

title: Floating macrophyte response diversity - stability mesocosm experiment
summary: We conducted a large mesocosm experiment with all combinations of 4 species of floating aquatic macrophytes. We exposed them to different nitrate concentrations and derived growth responses, then used response diversity per mesocosm as a predictor of temporal stability, and also resistance in response to an exogenous disturbance (a large typhoon).

title: Response diversity and slow environment exposure combine to explain and predict community stability
summary: We use simulated communities to ask when response diversity, the differences among species in how they respond to environmental change, stabilises community biomass. We show that this depends on how much environmental variation is slow relative to the community's own response times, which we call slow environment exposure.

title: Response diversity and the persistence of farmer-managed cardamom agroforestry in the eastern Himalaya
summary: Large cardamom grown under Alnus nepalensis canopy is a long-standing, multi-species agroforestry system in eastern Nepal and a major source of household income. Farmers report that cardamom performance is declining, even under canopy, and that production is moving to open land, while some households diversify their livelihoods and others abandon formerly productive land. This coupled social-ecological project asks whether variation in how the system’s components (plants, soil microbes, insects, patches and households) respond to shared gradients helps explain why some farms persist and others do not. The gradients we plan to use are canopy openness (light and heat exposure), soil conditions, disease and insect pressure, and market change. The functions of interest are cardamom production and household livelihood stability. We also ask how farmers update their management as evidence accumulates from their own experience, from other people, and from digital climate and market information, and how that updating shapes patch diversity. Fieldwork, including farmer perceptions, soil and tree measurements and linked plot data, is continuing as a pilot. Infrastructure for deeper study is limited, and we are seeking collaborators to help ground the work in response diversity theory and methods.
drivers: canopy loos and land use change, climate and temperature, soil conditions, disease and insect pests, market change, information
authorship_guidelines: Authorship will follow the CRediT contributor roles and will be discussed openly with any collaborator at the start.
